subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 1! In this unit you will become an expert on all the numbers from 0 to 1000. Last year you mastered the numbers up to 100. Now you are going to stretch that skill ten times further, all the way to one thousand. Three-digit numbers are all around you every single day. When Amina counts that there are 365 days until the next Eid, when Yusuf reads a book with 180 pages, or when Hassan lives at house number 321 on a busy Hargeisa street, they are all using numbers to 1000.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Read, write and represent numbers from 0 to 1000.
Say and show the value of each digit in a three-digit number (hundreds, tens and ones).
Write three-digit numbers in expanded form, for example 327 = 300 + 20 + 7.
Count on and back in steps of 1, 10 and 100 from any number.
Compare two three-digit numbers and use the symbols >, < and =.
Put a set of three-digit numbers in order from smallest to greatest and greatest to smallest.
Place numbers on a number line from 0 to 1000.
Make a sensible estimate of a quantity that cannot be counted exactly, giving the estimate as a believable range rather than a single guess.

concepts.title: What Is a Three-Digit Number?
concepts.explanation:
A three-digit number is any number from 100 up to 999. It is made of three digits, and each digit sits in its own place: the hundreds place, the tens place and the ones place. Just like a person’s address tells you exactly which house they live in, a digit’s place tells you exactly how much it is worth.

Let us look closely at the number 327. Reading from left to right:

The 3 is in the hundreds place, so it stands for 3 hundreds = 300.

The 2 is in the tens place, so it stands for 2 tens = 20.

The 7 is in the ones place, so it stands for 7 ones = 7.

Put the parts back together and you get 300 + 20 + 7 = 327. Writing a number this way – as the sum of its hundreds, tens and ones – is called expanded form, and it shows exactly what each digit is worth. Expanded form is one of the most useful tools in this whole unit, so practise it until it feels easy.

Three-digit numbers are everywhere once you start to look. There are 365 days in a year. Halima might live at house number 321. A storybook might have 180 pages. Nuur Academy might have 425 students walking through its gates each morning. Every one of these numbers is built from hundreds, tens and ones in exactly the way we have just seen.

It helps to picture the three places as three columns in a chart, with the largest value on the left and the smallest on the right. This is called a place value chart:
concepts.example: The top row shows the digits of 327; the bottom row shows what each digit is really worth. The chart makes it clear at a glance that the 3 is not just ‘three’ – it is three hundred. Whenever a number confuses you, drawing a quick place value chart is the fastest way to see it clearly.

concepts.title: Place Value – Why Position Is Everything
concepts.explanation:
This is the big idea of the whole unit, so let us slow right down. The position of a digit decides its value. The very same digit can mean completely different amounts depending on where it stands.

Look at the digit 5 in these three numbers:

In 500, the 5 is in the hundreds place, so it means five hundred.

In 50, the 5 is in the tens place, so it means fifty.

In 5, the 5 is in the ones place, so it means just five.

One digit, three totally different values – all because of its place. This is why place value matters so much. If Omar wants to write ‘five hundred and sixty-two’ but accidentally swaps the digits and writes 265, he has written a completely different number. He is off by nearly three hundred! Getting the places right is the difference between counting your camels correctly and losing track of the whole herd.

Now think about the special job of zero. In the number 504, there are 5 hundreds and 4 ones, but no tens. The zero is not lazy – it is doing an important job. It holds the tens place empty so that the 5 stays in the hundreds place and the 4 stays in the ones place. We call a zero used this way a place holder. Without it, 504 would collapse into 54, a completely different number. In 780 the zero holds the ones place, telling us there are 7 hundreds, 8 tens and no ones.

A good way to feel place value in your hands is to imagine base-ten blocks, the kind Sagal uses when she helps at Nuur Academy. A single small cube is one. A stick of ten cubes is one ten. A flat square of one hundred cubes is one hundred. To build 327, she lays out 3 flats, 2 sticks and 7 single cubes. To build 273 with the very same digits, she lays out 2 flats, 7 sticks and 3 cubes – a completely different pile, because the places have swapped. Try this yourself with stones, grouping them into hundreds, tens and ones, and you will never forget what place value means.
concepts.example: Let us practise reading the value of one chosen digit, because this is a favourite exam question. In 637, what is the value of the 3? The 3 sits in the tens place, so its value is 3 tens = 30. In 472, what is the value of the 7? The 7 sits in the tens place, so its value is 70. In 853, what is the value of the 8? The 8 sits in the hundreds place, so its value is 800. Always name the place first, then you will always name the value correctly.

concepts.title: Reading and Writing Numbers to 1000
concepts.explanation:
When we read a three-digit number, we say the hundreds first, then the tens and ones together. We usually pop in the little word ‘and’ after the hundreds. Let us look at three examples:

327 is read as “three hundred and twenty-seven”.

Reading a number out loud is one of the best ways to understand it. When you say “seven hundred and eighty” you can actually hear the hundreds, and you can hear that there is nothing in the ones place. Saying numbers aloud also helps you catch mistakes, so make it a habit whenever you meet a new number.

Writing numbers works both ways. Sometimes you start with digits and write the words; sometimes you start with words and write the digits. To turn words into digits, listen carefully for each place. ‘Three hundred and twenty-four’ gives you a 3 in the hundreds, a 2 in the tens and a 4 in the ones, so you write 324. ‘Eight hundred and ninety’ gives you 8 hundreds, 9 tens and no ones, so you write 890 – do not forget the place-holder zero. ‘One hundred and fifteen’ gives you 1 hundred, 1 ten and 5 ones, so you write 115.
concepts.example: Watch out for the tricky numbers between eleven and nineteen, and for the tens words. ‘Five hundred and seven’ is 507, not 5007 – the ‘seven’ is only 7 ones, and a zero must hold the empty tens place. Listening for which place each word belongs to keeps you from writing extra digits. When Khadija is unsure, she quietly says the number as hundreds, tens and ones before she writes a single digit.

concepts.title: Counting On and Back in 1s, 10s and 100s
concepts.explanation:
Counting one at a time is fine for small jumps, but slow for big ones. Smarter counting uses steps of 1, 10 and 100, and each step changes a different digit. Understanding which digit changes is the secret to counting quickly and confidently.

Counting on in ones changes the ones digit: 325, 326, 327, 328, 329 … When you pass a nine, the ones roll back to 0 and the tens go up by one: 329, 330, 331.

Counting on in tens changes the tens digit: 240, 250, 260, 270, 280. The ones digit stays the same and the hundreds stay the same, until you pass ninety, when the tens roll to 0 and the hundreds climb: 280, 290, 300, 310.

Counting on in hundreds changes the hundreds digit: 132, 232, 332, 432, 532. The tens and ones stay exactly the same the whole way – only the hundreds digit climbs by one each step. This is the fastest way to move a long distance along the number line.

Counting backwards works the same way, just in reverse. From 500 counting back in tens gives 500, 490, 480, 470, 460. From 640 counting back in hundreds gives 640, 540, 440, 340, 240. If Ibrahim has saved 340 shillings and spends one hundred, he does not count down one at a time – he jumps straight to 240. Knowing which digit each step controls turns slow counting into quick thinking.
concepts.example: Number strips help you see this. Imagine a strip torn from a 1-to-1000 number line showing … 478, 479, 480, 481 … To fill a gap, ask yourself what step the strip is counting in, then apply it. Zahra always checks two numbers she can already see to be sure of the step before she fills any blank.

concepts.title: Comparing Three-Digit Numbers
concepts.explanation:
To compare two numbers means to decide which is greater, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. With three-digit numbers the method is always the same, and it always starts from the left, because the left-hand digit is worth the most.

First compare the hundreds digit. The number with more hundreds is greater.

If the hundreds are the same, compare the tens digit.

If the tens are also the same, compare the ones digit.

Compare 375 and 475. Look at the hundreds: 3 against 4. Since 3 hundreds is less than 4 hundreds, we know 375 < 475 straight away. We did not even need to look at the tens or ones – the hundreds settled it.

Compare 682 and 678. The hundreds are the same (6 and 6), so move on to the tens: 8 against 7. Since 8 tens is more than 7 tens, 682 > 678. Once one place decides the answer, you can stop.

We write comparisons using three symbols. A helpful trick: the open, hungry mouth of the symbol always points at the bigger number, like a crocodile that always wants the larger meal.
concepts.example: A warning that catches many learners: a number is not automatically bigger just because one of its later digits is big. Compare 508 and 580. Both start with 5 hundreds, so we look at the tens: 508 has 0 tens while 580 has 8 tens. Because 8 tens beats 0 tens, 580 > 508, even though 508 ends in a large-looking 8. Always let the hundreds speak first, then the tens, then the ones. Never jump to the ones digit before you have checked the places above it.

concepts.title: Ordering Numbers and the Number Line
concepts.explanation:
To order a set of numbers means to line them up by size, usually from smallest to greatest (or sometimes greatest to smallest). You use exactly the same comparing method, just applied to the whole group.

Let us order these from smallest to greatest: 475, 679, 563, 621. Start with the hundreds digit of each. 475 has 4 hundreds, 563 has 5 hundreds, and both 621 and 679 have 6 hundreds. So the first two in order are 475, then 563. Now 621 and 679 both have 6 hundreds, so we look at their tens: 621 has 2 tens and 679 has 7 tens. Because 2 tens is less than 7 tens, 621 comes before 679. The final order is 475, 563, 621, 679.

A careful method that never fails: find the smallest number in the list and write it down, cross it off, then find the smallest of what remains, and repeat until every number is placed. Working this way stops you from missing a number or putting one in the wrong spot. To order from greatest to smallest, simply pick the largest each time instead.

A number line is a wonderful picture for ordering. Imagine the long road from Mogadishu to a distant town, with a signpost every hundred kilometres: 0, 100, 200, 300, all the way to 1000. Every three-digit number has its own place on this road. Numbers on the left are smaller; numbers on the right are larger.

To place 475 on this line, first find the stretch it belongs to. It is between 400 and 500, because it has 4 hundreds. Then decide where in that stretch: 475 is past the halfway mark of 450, so it sits closer to 500 than to 400. Placing numbers on a line helps you see how big they are and how far apart two numbers really are. Here is a simple picture of the whole road:
concepts.example: A careful method that never fails: find the smallest number in the list and write it down, cross it off, then find the smallest of what remains, and repeat until every number is placed. Working this way stops you from… Sometimes you cannot count something exactly, and you do not need to – you only need a sensible estimate. Imagine a jar full of dried dates, or a crowd gathered outside the masjid: counting one by one would take too long, so instead you make a sensible estimate, which is a careful guess based on what you can see, given as a range rather than one exact number. A good way to do this is to count a small, easy part first, then use it to judge the rest. For example, if you can see that one layer of dates fills about 20 dates, and the jar looks like it could hold roughly 8 to 10 layers, then a sensible estimate is somewhere between 160 and 200 dates – not an exact number, but a believable range. A sensible estimate should never be wildly too big or too small: if you guessed the jar held 5 dates or 5000 dates, that would not be sensible, because it does not match what your eyes and your reasoning tell you. Estimating as a range like this is a different skill from rounding a number you already know exactly – it is about making a smart judgement when an exact count is not possible or not needed.

methods.title: How to write a number in expanded form
methods.example: What is the value of the 6 in the number 462?
steps: Find the value of the hundreds digit (for example, 3 → 300).
Find the value of the tens digit (for example, 2 → 20).
Find the value of the ones digit (for example, 7 → 7).
Join them with plus signs: 300 + 20 + 7.

methods.title: How to compare two numbers
steps: Compare the hundreds digit of each number.
If one has more hundreds, that number is greater — stop.
If the hundreds are equal, compare the tens; if the tens are equal, compare the ones.
Write the correct symbol: >, < or =.

methods.title: Decide first: nearest 10 or nearest 100?
methods.example: Write ‘five hundred and four’ in digits.
steps: For the nearest 10, look at the ones digit; for the nearest 100, look at the tens digit.
If that digit is 5 or more, round up to the next ten or hundred.
If it is 4 or less, round down to the ten or hundred below.

methods.title: Comparing
steps: Both have 7 hundreds, so compare the tens.
719 has 1 ten; 791 has 9 tens.
Since 9 tens beats 1 ten, 791 > 719.
The crocodile mouth opens towards 791.

methods.title: Ordering
methods.example: Put these camel counts in order from smallest to greatest: 608, 680, 860, 806, 686.
steps: Compare hundreds first: 608, 680, 686 have 6 hundreds; 806 has 8 hundreds; 860 has 8 hundreds.
So the three 6-hundreds numbers come first.
Among 608, 680, 686 the hundreds are equal, so compare tens: 608 has 0 tens, 680 has 8 tens, 686 has 8 tens.
So 608 is first; then between 680 and 686 the tens are equal, so compare ones — 0 against 6 — so 680 then 686.

methods.title: Rounding to the nearest 10
steps: Look at the ones digit: 7.
Since 7 is 5 or more, round up.
The ten below is 900 and the next ten is 910, so 907 rounds to 910.

workedExamples.title: The value of a digit
workedExamples.prompt: What is the value of the 6 in the number 462?
workedExamples.solution: Name the place first. The 6 sits in the tens place. So its value is 6 tens = 60. (The 4 is worth 400 and the 2 is worth 2, and indeed 400 + 60 + 2 = 462.)

workedExamples.title: Expanded form
workedExamples.solution: Break it into places. 8 hundreds = 800, 1 ten = 10, 9 ones = 9. So 819 = 800 + 10 + 9. Notice each part shows the true value of its digit.

workedExamples.title: Words to digits with a place holder
workedExamples.prompt: Write ‘five hundred and four’ in digits.
workedExamples.solution: Listen for each place. Five hundred gives a 5 in the hundreds. There is no tens word, so the tens place needs a place-holder 0. ‘Four’ gives a 4 in the ones. The number is 504. Forgetting the zero would wrongly give 54.

workedExamples.title: Comparing
workedExamples.solution: Both have 7 hundreds, so compare the tens. 719 has 1 ten; 791 has 9 tens. Since 9 tens beats 1 ten, 791 > 719. The crocodile mouth opens towards 791.

workedExamples.title: Ordering
workedExamples.prompt: Put these camel counts in order from smallest to greatest: 608, 680, 860, 806, 686.
workedExamples.solution: Compare hundreds first: 608, 680, 686 have 6 hundreds; 806 has 8 hundreds; 860 has 8 hundreds. So the three 6-hundreds numbers come first. Among 608, 680, 686 the hundreds are equal, so compare tens: 608 has 0 tens, 680 has 8 tens, 686 has 8 tens. So 608 is first; then between 680 and 686 the tens are equal, so compare ones — 0 against 6 — so 680 then 686. Now the 8-hundreds numbers: 806 has 0 tens, 860 has 6 tens, so 806 then 860. Final order: 608, 680, 686, 806, 860.

workedExamples.title: Rounding to the nearest 10
workedExamples.solution: Look at the ones digit: 7. Since 7 is 5 or more, round up. The ten below is 900 and the next ten is 910, so 907 rounds to 910.

workedExamples.title: Rounding to the nearest 100
workedExamples.solution: Look at the tens digit: 4. Since 4 is 4 or less, round down. The hundred below is 600 and the next hundred is 700, so 648 rounds to 600. (Careful: do not be fooled by the 8 in the ones — for the nearest 100 we look only at the tens.)

workedExamples.title: Estimating a sum by rounding
workedExamples.prompt: Estimate 328 + 271 by rounding each number to the nearest 10.
workedExamples.solution: 328 rounds to 330 (ones digit 8, round up). 271 rounds to 270 (ones digit 1, round down). So the estimate is 330 + 270 = 600. The real answer is 599, so our estimate is excellent — that is how we know it makes sense.

workedExamples.prompt: Round each to the nearest 10: a) 23 b) 385 c) 599 d) 740.

workedExamples.title: Round each to the nearest 100
workedExamples.prompt: Round each to the nearest 100: a) 123 b) 678 c) 950.

activities.title: Place Value Detective
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and three dice (or number cards 0–9).
steps: Roll the three dice to make a three-digit number (choose an order for the digits).
Write the number down, then draw a place value chart showing hundreds, tens and ones.
Write the value of each digit, and then write the whole number in expanded form.
Write the number in words.
Repeat five times, then challenge yourself: with your three digits, make the largest and the smallest three-digit number possible.

activities.title: Build It With Bundles (Base-Ten)
activities.materials: a big pile of small stones, sticks or dry beans, and some string or rubber bands.
steps: Make some ‘hundreds’ by tying ten bundles of ten together, some ‘tens’ by tying ten singles together, and keep some loose ‘ones’.
Ask a family member to call out a three-digit number under 1000.
Build it using hundreds, tens and ones – for example, 327 is 3 hundreds, 2 tens and 7 ones.
Say the expanded form out loud: three hundred plus twenty plus seven.
Now swap two of the digits and build the new number. Talk about how much the value changed.

activities.title: The Crocodile Compare Game
activities.materials: paper cards, each with a three-digit number you write yourself (make about twenty).
steps: Shuffle the cards and place them face down in a pile.
Each player turns over one card.
Draw a crocodile mouth (> or <) pointing at the greater number, saying why using place value.
The player with the greater number keeps both cards.
Play until the cards run out. The player with the most cards wins.

activities.title: Rounding Race to the Nearest 100
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and your number cards from Activity 3.
steps: Draw a number line and mark the hundreds: 0, 100, 200 … up to 1000.
Turn over a card and place the number roughly where it belongs on the line.
Decide which hundred it is closest to, and round it there. Check with the tens-digit rule.
Do the same for rounding to the nearest 10 on a smaller line.
Keep score: one point each time you and a partner agree on the correct rounding.

activities.title: Estimation Station (Investigation)
activities.materials: a container and lots of small objects (beans, buttons, bottle caps).
steps: Put a large handful of objects in the container.
Estimate how many there are, and write your estimate down as a sensible guess.
Count them by grouping into tens, then into hundreds, then counting the groups.
Compare your estimate to the true count. How close were you?
Repeat three times with different amounts and see whether your estimates get better.

activities.title: Number Line Hop (Family Game)
activities.materials: chalk or a long strip of paper, and your family or friends.
steps: Draw a big number line on the ground from 0 to 1000, marking every 100.
Call out a three-digit number, and have a player hop to roughly where it belongs.
The others say whether it is closer to the hundred below or the hundred above.
Now call out numbers to order: three players each take a number and line themselves up smallest to greatest.
Talk about how the number line and place value always agree.

rules.title: Place Value Rule
rules.text: Left digit = hundreds. Middle digit = tens. Right digit = ones. 327 = 3 hundreds + 2 tens + 7 ones = 300 + 20 + 7. A zero is a place holder: it keeps a place empty, like the 0 in 504.

rules.title: Comparing Rule
rules.text: Compare the hundreds first. More hundreds = greater number. If the hundreds are equal, compare the tens. If the tens are equal, compare the ones. The open mouth of > or < always points at the bigger number.

rules.title: Rounding Rule
rules.text: To the nearest 10, look at the ones digit. To the nearest 100, look at the tens digit. If that digit is 5 or more, round up. If it is 4 or less, round down. Example: 648 rounds to 650 to the nearest 10, and to 600 to the nearest 100.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Ordering Numbers and the Number Line.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To order a set of numbers means to line them up by size, usually from smallest to greatest (or sometimes greatest to smallest). You use exactly the same comparing method, just applied to the whole group. Let us order these from smallest to greatest: 475, 679, 563, 621. Start with the hundreds digit of each. 475 has 4 hundreds, 563 has 5 hundreds, and both 621 and 679 have 6 hundreds. So the first two in order are 475, then 563. Now 621 and 679 both have 6 hundreds, so we look at their tens: 621 has 2 tens and 679 has 7 tens, so 621 comes before 679. Final order: 475, 563, 621, 679.
